title: Quantum mechanics I
tagline: Wavefunctions, operators and the hydrogen atom
summary: The experimental origins, the Schrödinger equation, piecewise potentials, the harmonic oscillator, the formal theory, angular momentum, hydrogen and spin.
overview: Quantum mechanics replaces the trajectory of a particle by a complex wavefunction $\Psi$, whose squared modulus is a probability density, and replaces position, momentum and energy by operators. The Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t\Psi = \hat H\Psi$ is the equation of motion. Almost every exact solution an undergraduate meets is in this course: the infinite and finite square wells, the step and the barrier, the harmonic oscillator, the rigid rotor and the hydrogen atom, together with the two-state system of spin one-half.

The course begins with the experiments that broke classical physics (black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, atomic spectra and electron diffraction) and does each calculation with real numbers. Three chapters of wave mechanics in one dimension follow, where quantisation, reflection and tunnelling can be seen without the complication of angular momentum. The formal chapter then states what a state, an observable and a measurement are, and proves the uncertainty principle, so that angular momentum, hydrogen and spin appear as applications of a single structure rather than as three separate tricks.

The hard part is not the mathematics, which is linear algebra and second-order differential equations, but learning to read it. Keep separate a stationary state, whose probability density is frozen, and a superposition, which moves at the Bohr frequencies; an expectation value and a measured result; a commutator and a product. Check normalisation and boundary conditions every time, and estimate before you calculate: comparing $h\nu$ with $k_BT$, or a de Broglie wavelength with the size of the system, tells you whether quantum effects matter at all.
outcomes: Explain how black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering and atomic spectra contradict classical physics, and compute the quantities involved with Planck's constant.
Normalise a wavefunction, compute probabilities, expectation values, uncertainties and probability currents, and use Ehrenfest's theorem.
Separate the time-dependent Schrödinger equation into stationary states and expand a given initial state in energy eigenfunctions to find its time evolution.
Solve the time-independent Schrödinger equation for piecewise constant potentials, including the transcendental equation of the finite well and the transmission coefficient of a barrier.
Derive the spectrum and eigenfunctions of the harmonic oscillator with ladder operators and with the power-series method.
Use Dirac notation, Hermitian operators and the measurement postulates, and prove the Robertson uncertainty relation.
Derive the eigenvalues of angular momentum from its commutation relations, and use spherical harmonics and the rules for adding two angular momenta.
Solve the hydrogen atom for its energy levels, degeneracies and low-lying wavefunctions, and compute spectral lines with the reduced mass.
Describe spin one-half with Pauli matrices, predict Stern–Gerlach outcomes along arbitrary axes, follow Larmor precession, and form triplet and singlet states.

history.title: Planck's quantum
history.detail: On 14 December 1900 Max Planck presented a derivation of the black-body spectrum in which the energy of an oscillator of frequency ν comes in multiples of hν.

history.title: Light quanta
history.detail: Einstein proposed that light is absorbed and emitted in quanta of energy hν and predicted the linear law of the photoelectric effect, which Millikan confirmed in 1916.

history.title: Bohr's atom
history.detail: Niels Bohr combined Rutherford's nuclear atom with quantised orbits and derived the Rydberg constant of hydrogen from e, m and h.

history.title: Stern–Gerlach experiment
history.detail: A beam of silver atoms passed through an inhomogeneous magnetic field split into two discrete spots, showing that the component of the atomic magnetic moment is quantised.

history.title: Compton scattering
history.detail: Arthur Compton measured the increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons and explained it by photons carrying momentum h/λ.

history.title: Matter waves
history.detail: Louis de Broglie's thesis assigned a wavelength h/p to every particle; Davisson and Germer, and independently G. P. Thomson, observed electron diffraction in 1927.

history.title: Matrix mechanics and spin
history.detail: Heisenberg's paper of July 1925, developed with Born and Jordan, founded matrix mechanics; in November Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit proposed that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum ħ/2.

history.title: Wave mechanics and the Born rule
history.detail: Schrödinger published his wave equation and solved hydrogen with it; Born proposed that the squared modulus of the wavefunction is a probability.

history.title: Uncertainty and Pauli matrices
history.detail: Heisenberg published the uncertainty relations, Kennard proved Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2, and Pauli gave the two-component theory of electron spin.

history.title: Hilbert space
history.detail: John von Neumann's Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik gave the theory its rigorous formulation in terms of self-adjoint operators on Hilbert space.

references.title: Introduction to Quantum Mechanics
references.authors: David J. Griffiths and Darrell F. Schroeter
references.note: Third edition. The standard first course, which this one follows closely; clear derivations and excellent problems.

references.title: Principles of Quantum Mechanics
references.note: Second edition. Opens with the linear algebra of Hilbert space and is the best companion to the formalism chapter; thorough on the oscillator and angular momentum.

references.title: A Modern Approach to Quantum Mechanics
references.note: Second edition. Starts from spin and Stern–Gerlach experiments and builds the formalism from two-state systems; a good alternative order.

references.title: Modern Quantum Mechanics
references.authors: J. J. Sakurai and Jim Napolitano
references.note: Third edition. The graduate-level sequel; its first chapters on Stern–Gerlach, Dirac notation and angular momentum deepen this course.

references.title: Quantum Mechanics
references.authors: B. H. Bransden and C. J. Joachain
references.note: Second edition. More detail on the experimental origins, the hydrogen atom and one-dimensional problems, with many worked examples.

references.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume III
references.authors: Richard P. Feynman, Robert B. Leighton and Matthew Sands
references.note: Quantum mechanics from amplitudes and spin; read it for physical insight alongside a more systematic text.
